strengths: The paper addresses a clearly identified and well-motivated gap: distractor-free radiance field research has grown rapidly (Fig. 3) but lacked a large-scale public dataset with paired clean/cluttered images per scene. The literature analysis (Tabs. 1-2) is thorough and fairly positions the work against prior and concurrent datasets, including acknowledging concurrent efforts (RealX3D, D-RE10K-iPhone).

The dataset itself is substantial for its declared contribution type (Datasets/Benchmarks): 1,048 real-world scenes (726 indoor / 322 outdoor), 89,924 images, 128 distractor types, 161 themes, 12 devices, collected over 9 months (~2 GPU-years of benchmarking alone). The systematic design of DF3DV-41 with 17 curated distractor/scene scenarios (Fig. 4) enables scenario-wise robustness analysis rather than only aggregate scores.

The benchmark is comprehensive: ten open-source methods evaluated across 1,048 scenes plus RobustNeRF and On-the-go, with a useful difficulty analysis via per-image metric distributions (Fig. 5) and identification of concrete failure modes (semantically similar/fluid distractors, nighttime scenes) with plausible technical explanations.

The DI2FIX experiment strengthens the contribution beyond curation: it demonstrates that the dataset enables progress beyond scene-specific methods (0.96 dB PSNR, 0.057 LPIPS improvement as a plug-and-play enhancer), with sensible ablations on training-scale (Tab. 5), pair-filtering threshold (Tab. 6), a leave-one-method-out OOD test (Tab. S.5), and baseline comparisons showing naive fine-tuning on RobustNeRF is insufficient (Tab. 4).

The data collection and curation pipeline (Fig. 6) is described in reproducible detail: controlled capture protocols, joint COLMAP pose estimation on clean+cluttered images, instant-ngp verification, and manual metadata annotation. A clear limitations section is included.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is underspecified in the main text. It is unclear how test views are selected relative to clean/cluttered image sets, whether poses of test views come from the joint COLMAP solution (which uses clean views and could bias evaluation), and how per-scene train/test splits are defined for the 1,048-scene benchmark. These details matter for interpreting absolute numbers and should be made explicit.

Potential circularity in difficulty design: the 128 distractor types and DF3DV-41 scenarios were designed by the authors with knowledge of how current methods fail (e.g., semantically similar distractors targeting feature-based segmentation). While defensible for a stress-test benchmark, the paper does not discuss the risk that rankings on DF3DV-1K may not generalize to distractor distributions outside the authors' taxonomy.

Taxonomy statistics (128 distractor types, 161 themes, 17 scenarios) rely on subjective manual annotation with no inter-annotator agreement or validation reported; the metadata quality that underpins the scenario-wise analysis is not quantitatively verified.

DI2FIX improves PSNR and LPIPS consistently but yields limited SSIM changes, and detailed per-method results (Tabs. S.4, S.5) and most scenario-wise analyses are relegated to supplementary material not provided for review, making it hard to verify some claims (e.g., 'consistently improves every method').

For a dataset release, data governance is not discussed: licensing terms, image consent (many outdoor scenes presumably contain bystanders and private property), and redistribution rights are unaddressed, which is a relevant societal consideration for manually captured data at this scale.

The 'ranking follows publication timeline' observation is presented as evidence of benchmark reliability, but with 10 methods and correlated design lineages it is a weak signal; rankings on prior benchmarks are noted to differ, so more analysis (e.g., statistical significance of rank differences) would strengthen the claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: distractor-free radiance field research has outgrown the small RobustNeRF (5 scenes) and On-the-go (12 scenes) benchmarks, and the community clearly lacks a large-scale resource with paired clean/cluttered image sets per scene.

The scale of the data collection effort is substantial: 1,048 manually captured indoor/outdoor scenes, ~90K images, 128 distractor types, 161 themes, 12 consumer devices, collected over nine months, which credibly mimics casual capture conditions better than prior curated benchmarks.

DF3DV-41 with 17 systematically designed distractor/scene scenarios is a thoughtful addition, enabling scenario-wise robustness analysis rather than only aggregate metrics; the analysis identifying semantically similar, fluid, and nighttime cases as failure modes is informative.

The benchmark across ten methods on ~1,048 scenes (~2 GPU-years of compute) is a comprehensive and reproducibility-friendly evaluation, and the paper is candid that existing benchmarks have become saturated for recent methods.

The ablations for DI²FIX (training scale, degradation threshold, leave-one-method-out OOD test) are reasonable, and the limitations section is honest about residual cloud movement in clean images and DI²FIX failure modes.
weaknesses: The contribution type is Datasets/Benchmarks, but the paper's scientific novelty beyond scale is limited. The dataset construction pipeline (scene design, COLMAP poses, instant-ngp verification, manual annotation) is a straightforward engineering effort; DI²FIX is a fine-tuning of an existing off-the-shelf enhancer (DIFIX) with a reference-view substitution, which reads more like a pilot application than a technical contribution. The overall package is 'big collection + existing methods + fine-tuned existing model,' which dilutes the scientific case relative to the large resource investment.

Ground-truth validity is under-examined. Evaluation appears to use clean images as reference views, but the paper itself admits cloud movement and other subtle appearance drift can contaminate clean captures. At 17.9-20.5 dB PSNR operating range on DF3DV-1K, it is unclear how much of the measured 'difficulty' reflects true distractor robustness versus noise from capture-time appearance changes, JPEG compression, or exposure drift between clean and cluttered passes (operators may adjust exposure/focus mid-capture). No controlled experiment quantifies this confound.

The claimed finding that 'rankings follow publication timeline' is presented as evidence of benchmark reliability, but it is close to circular: newer methods are trained/tuned on similar casual-capture data distributions, and the claim risks showing recency rather than robustness. The paper does not disentangle these, and the observation that rankings flip across datasets is left largely uninterpreted.

Benchmark fairness and protocol details are thin. For ten per-scene-optimization methods across 1,048 scenes, the paper does not clarify how per-method hyperparameters were selected (default settings from original papers?), how much per-scene tuning was permitted, or variance across runs of stochastic 3DGS training. Differences among the top methods (e.g., 20.49 vs 20.13 dB PSNR) may not be significant without such analysis.

The headline DI²FIX improvement (0.96 dB PSNR, 0.057 LPIPS) is modest, and SSIM is roughly unchanged or slightly improved, which the authors acknowledge reflects a perceptual trade-off. The practical value of a plug-in enhancer that can also 'mistakenly modify static content' (as shown in their own ablations and limitations) is not convincingly established.

The empirical claim that prior benchmarks are 'saturated' and require 'zoom-in' comparisons rests substantially on citing figures from other papers rather than a rigorous difficulty measure; the difficulty analysis in Fig. 5 relies on vanilla 3DGS behavior, which conflates scene difficulty with reconstruction quality.

Significant related resources are concurrent and non-released (RealX3D, D-RE10K-iPhone, the ICLR'26 generalizable method), making it hard to verify DF3DV-1K's claimed uniqueness; comparisons to these concurrent works are necessarily qualitative, and the field may be crowded by the time of publication.

Clarity issues: Table 1/Table 2 contain inconsistencies with cited sources (e.g., scene counts for RobustNeRF), several statements about datasets 'not released yet' or 'March 2026' will age poorly, and key details needed for reproduction (exact train/test view splits, whether test views come from clean or cluttered sets, licensing and release terms of the 90K-image dataset captured by identifiable operators) are relegated to supplementary material or omitted.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly documented gap: existing distractor-free radiance field benchmarks (RobustNeRF, On-the-go) are small and saturated, and the authors convincingly show via Table 2 and the surrounding analysis that no public, large-scale dataset with paired clean/cluttered images per scene exists. The motivating argument (Figs. 1-3, Table 1) is thorough and fair to prior work.

The dataset is substantial: 1,048 scenes, ~90K images, 128 distractor types, 161 themes, indoor and outdoor coverage, collected over nine months with consumer devices to mimic casual capture. The systematic design (Fig. 6) - predefined themes, controlled capture protocols, COLMAP pose estimation with joint clean/cluttered registration, instant-ngp-based verification, and manual metadata annotation - follows and extends established curation practice.

The benchmark is broad and useful: ten methods evaluated across all 1,048 scenes plus a systematically designed 41-scene subset (DF3DV-41) with 17 scenario categories. The finding that rankings track publication timelines and differ across datasets supports the claim that a harder benchmark is needed, and the scenario-wise analysis (semantically similar/fluid distractors, nighttime scenes) yields actionable insights about why current methods fail.

The DI2FIX application is a well-chosen demonstration that the dataset enables progress beyond per-scene optimization: fine-tuning DIFIX yields consistent gains (0.96 dB PSNR, 0.057 LPIPS) with sensible ablations on training scale (Table 5), degradation filtering threshold (Table 6), and a leave-one-method-out OOD test (Table S.5) supporting generalization.

The work is positioned honestly: the authors acknowledge that prior benchmarks are not flawed but simply outpaced, list concurrent efforts (RealX3D, D-RE10K-iPhone) and compare against them, and include a limitations section (capture cost, residual cloud motion, DI2FIX failure modes).

As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the paper is appropriately judged on scale, curation quality, difficulty, and downstream utility rather than novel algorithmics, and it performs well on all of these axes.
weaknesses: Dataset difficulty could be confounded. The claim that DF3DV-1K is 'more challenging' rests partly on lower 3DGS PSNR/LPIPS, but lower scores could also stem from blur, low light, or textureless content rather than distractor robustness per se. The difficulty analysis (Fig. 5) is suggestive but not a controlled comparison; a distractor-free ablation on the same scenes would strengthen the claim.

Potential privacy and release concerns are under-addressed. The dataset contains casually captured indoor/outdoor scenes with passersby and dynamic people (e.g., 'daily scenes', 'passer-by' scenarios). The manuscript does not discuss consent, anonymization, licensing terms, or an explicit public release mechanism/URL, which is a significant omission for a dataset paper and affects reproducibility.

Annotation and data-quality verification are described only qualitatively. 'Two experts per scene' reviewed data, but there is no inter-annotator agreement, error rate, or quantitative check that clean images are truly distractor-free; given that clean images serve as ground truth for PSNR/LPIPS, residual distractor contamination would bias all benchmark numbers.

Benchmark fairness details are thin in the main text. Running ten per-scene optimization methods across 1,048 scenes requires per-method hyperparameter choices; the paper does not clarify how settings were selected (default configurations vs. tuned per dataset), which could disadvantage some methods and affect the ranking claims.

The DI2FIX evaluation protocol has a subtle leakage concern: training pairs are constructed by rendering novel views at clean-image viewpoints of training scenes, and evaluation uses clean-image viewpoints of held-out scenes. This is standard, but the metric gains are modest for SSIM (which the authors attribute to the perception-distortion tradeoff) and the enhancer is only validated on a small set of base renderings; its effect on the weakest-performing scenarios (nighttime, fluid) is not isolated.

Some claims rely heavily on supplementary material (Tabs. S.1-3, S.4-5, Figs. S.1-S.16) that is not fully verifiable from the main paper, and Table 3 gains over 3DGS on DF3DV-1K (~2.5 dB) are smaller than on prior benchmarks, which slightly weakens the narrative that the new benchmark better differentiates methods.

Table 2 mixes released, unpublished, and 'not published yet (March 2026)' datasets, and the field moves quickly (e.g., Wildrayzer, distractor-free generalizable 3DGS at ICLR 2026); the paper should more carefully defend its timing claims relative to these concurrent resources.
